# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It runs context, then problem, then solution, then pilot and sending, which is how I would explain Expanse to a stranger: researchers guessing sizes at submit, the jobs that die or waste the cluster, then the submit-time prediction.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context step reads as asked twice unless the two screens visibly cover different fields; screen 2's 'Where are the people who would buy this?' also overlaps the context's where (US).
founder.missing: Nothing asks who pays or what it costs: the researcher is the one who suffers, but the cluster operator (or a department running the pilot) pays per cluster a month ($10,000 to $20,000 by my reading), and the security review of an agent on every node is the real purchase hurdle. The flow never asks for the payer, the price, the existing cost (30% to 59% of GPU hours wasted) or that friction.

PRIMARY.order_why: The question about whether my job's source code was on the cluster reads like a setup question about my last job, so it belongs in Part 1 with the recent-time questions, not after the idea card.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the scheduler killed my job (out of memory, out of time, or preempted), how much work I lost, how much I usually pad memory, GPUs and run time when I submit, and how I currently guess those numbers.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it checks the one thing that makes me fit, a shared cluster big enough to matter, so it's obvious why it comes first.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes and GPU count are everyday words in my work, and I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many GPUs our shared cluster has from sinfo and the partition list, and 100 is far enough from ours that I wouldn't be guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a gate with no escape, and the true answer is always one of the two.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, SLURM or Kubernetes with 100 or more GPUs, and nothing of a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: The question is short and says well, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky against §17's plain 'Yes or no.' for a screener.
screens.instead: Do any of the SLURM or Kubernetes clusters you work on have 100 or more GPUs? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a 100+ GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine got killed this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Job killed by the scheduler" is exactly how we talk about SLURM jobs dying, so I'd answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether any of my jobs got killed in the last week; I see the sacct state and the email.
screens.why4: Yes or No is complete and distinct for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed mid-run because I under-requested memory or time, but "killed by the scheduler" also catches preemption by a higher-priority job, and some OOM kills come from the cgroup, not the scheduler, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why6: One short question, then "Yes or no"; easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Both Yes and No are true of someone, so the gate is healthy, but dropping the under-request condition lets a preempted job count as Yes, which bends the rule that the gate asks the founder's problem.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a job killed for running out of memory or past its time limit? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether the scheduler killed one of my jobs, showing an idea about predicting a job's resources at submit time makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Most of it is how I talk (walltime, GPU memory, SLURM), but "every node of your network" is odd: I work on a cluster, not a network, and the nodes aren't mine to install on.
screens.why3: Guessing memory, GPUs and walltime before I submit, and losing a run when I guess low, is exactly what I do every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks that shouldn't, but "network" where the setting is clearly a shared GPU cluster reads like a small drift from the founder's words.
screens.why6: It is long when heard, and "GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime" is said twice; the bare "memory, memory" trips the ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, software on your cluster that predicts each job's resources when you submit it. It reads your code, script and hardware, then predicts GPU memory, system RAM, CPUs and walltime and warns of failures before they happen. It also suggests optimisations line by line and explains why a job failed and how to fix it. The people building it believe it would give each job exactly what it needs.

screens.why1: A question about fitting into how I already work belongs right after the Expanse card, but whether my code sits on the cluster has nothing to do with predicting memory, GPUs and run time at submit, so it comes across as abrupt.
screens.why2: 'Had your job's source code sitting on the cluster?' has lost its subject and verb order, so I had to read it twice to see it means 'Was your job's code on the cluster?'
screens.why3: I know exactly where my fine-tuning code lived when I submitted it, so I can answer this from my own last job.
screens.why4: Three options plus 'I can't tell' is right for a fact, but 'Yes, with some steps' is odd for whether my code was simply there; it was or it wasn't, unless I count a git pull or a container build.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks past the card, but the condition reads as clipped from a founder's phrase and has lost its subject, so it has likely drifted from what was typed.
screens.why6: The list and the escape say well, but the broken stem 'Had your job's source code sitting on the cluster?' sounds wrong heard once and makes me stop on the question itself.
screens.why7: This is a condition the segment already settles: anyone submitting jobs on a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster has their code or image there, so every answer is Yes, nothing can count against the belief, and the step the prediction depends on (past usage records, or letting it set the requests) is not tested.
screens.instead: On your last job, did the cluster keep a record of the memory, GPUs and time earlier runs of it actually used? Yes · Yes, with some steps · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the source-code check, asking whether Expanse would have done better for me is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I had to read 'the most recent time you had to get each job to run to the end' twice, because 'each job' in one moment makes no sense and 'done that' leaves me unsure what Expanse is meant to have done.
screens.why3: Every job I submit is a time I want it to run to the end, so this points at no particular submit, and I'd be guessing which one to judge rather than recalling the one where I had to guess memory and GPUs, or got killed for it.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse are distinct, cover the true answers, and the I-can't-tell chip fits.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product leaks beyond the card, but the founder's own job phrase 'get each job to run to the end' is pasted in verbatim, and it is not how I'd say it.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list of four with one escape, but 'get each job to run to the end' and 'done that' is a mouthful that doesn't land on one hearing.

screens.why1: Coming last after the idea and whether it would do better, asking if I'd actually trust its numbers over my own padding is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Padding requests is exactly what we all do on SLURM, so 'use the suggested sizes instead of padding your requests' reads plain to me on the first pass.
screens.why3: I size every job I submit myself, so whether I'd drop my padding for its numbers is something only I can answer.
screens.why4: 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' is just a softer Yes; my real catch is getting killed mid-run and losing days of work, and no option names that.
screens.why5: 'Suggested sizes' follows from the card's 'predicts each job's resources' and nothing of the founder's own terms reaches me outside the idea card.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options I can hold, then the one escape, so it says well.
screens.why7: The effort is mine and the measure, order, balance and escape all hold, but the conditional is the fixed fallback rather than my own condition, so it blurs into Yes and hides the risk the card warns of.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd use the suggested sizes instead of padding your requests. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if my job wouldn't get killed mid-run · Probably not · No · I can't tell
